title: CarbonClarity: Understanding and Addressing Uncertainty in Embodied Carbon for Sustainable Computing
problem: Deterministic embodied carbon models fail to account for spatial and temporal variability in semiconductor supply chain, limiting carbon-aware design decisions.
motivation: Embodied carbon is a significant contributor to computing's carbon footprint; uncertainty quantification enables informed design choices.
method: The framework treats embodied carbon—carbon emitted during chip manufacturing—as probability distributions (ranges of likely values) rather than single fixed numbers, accounting for where and when a chip is made. It models how four key factors vary by location and time: energy-per-area (factory electricity per unit of chip space), gas-per-area (manufacturing gas emissions per unit of chip space), yield (percentage of working chips produced), and carbon intensity (cleanness of the power source), doing this separately for each technology node (manufacturing scale like 5nm, 7nm, etc.). The team validated the framework by comparing two chip designs—chiplet architectures (multiple smaller chips connected together) and monolithic architectures (one large chip)—to determine which produces lower embodied carbon when accounting for real-world uncertainty.
key_novelty: It's the first embodied carbon model that captures how supply chain uncertainty varies across different manufacturing scales by treating carbon as probability distributions rather than single fixed numbers.
contributions: Probabilistic framework for embodied carbon with uncertainty distributions
Quantification of embodied carbon variance across technology nodes
Evaluation of chiplet vs monolithic design carbon impact and uncertainty
Device provisioning methodology under carbon budget constraints

metrics.other: 1.6x gap between mean and 95th percentile carbon at 7nm; 18% uncertainty reduction for chiplets

limitations: Focuses on embodied carbon only, not operational carbon; assumes supply chain data accuracy; case studies limited to specific architectures.
